title_en: The Ethics Problem in Financial Services (Dr. Moira Somers & Philippa Hann) | #425
title_zh: 金融服务中的伦理困境（Dr. Moira Somers 与 Philippa Hann）
subtitle_zh: 第 425 期。Ben Felix 与 Cameron Passmore 对话 Philippa Hann 和临床神经心理学家 Dr. Moira Somers，聊她们合著的新书以及金融业里的不当行为、心理变态者与道德盲区。
description: The Ethics Problem in Financial Services (Dr. Moira Somers & Philippa Hann) | #425

turns.en: This is a good person doing bad things. People who have lots of money are amazing prey for people who want to get down. And I mean, I met some psychopaths.
turns.zh: 这是个好人做了坏事。有钱人正是那些想坑蒙拐骗者眼里的绝佳猎物。我是说，我真遇到过几个精神病态者（psychopath）。

turns.en: Welcome to Episode 425 of the Raster Minder podcast. Today, we're joined by Philippa Hahn and Dr. Moira Summers, who are co-authors of a new book, The Fault Lines of Finance, Understanding and Preventing Financial Misconduct.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听《Rational Reminder》播客第425期。今天我们请到 Philippa Hann 和 Moira Somers 博士，两人合著了一本新书《The Fault Lines of Finance: Understanding and Preventing Financial Misconduct》（《金融的断层线：理解并预防金融不当行为》）。

turns.en: Philippa Hahn is a lawyer who spent two decades been suing financial advisors, including over a thousand claims on behalf of British steelworkers who lost their pensions.
turns.zh: Philippa Hann 是一名律师，二十年来一直在起诉金融顾问，其中包括代表失去养老金的英国钢铁工人提起的逾一千起索赔。

turns.en: And Dr. Moira Summers, longtime friend of ours, is a clinical neuropsychologist who coaches financial professionals on the human side of money.
turns.zh: 而我们的老朋友 Moira Somers 博士是一名临床神经心理学家，她在金钱的人性层面方面指导金融专业人士。

turns.en: And I'm sure many listeners will remember her from episodes 45 and 92 when she joined us with Dave Getch. Yeah, longtime friend of the firm and now a three-time guest.
turns.zh: 我相信很多听众会从第45期和第92期记得她，那时她和 Dave Getch 一起参加我们的节目。是啊，她是本公司的老朋友，如今已是三度做客。

turns.en: Not too many of those out there. We talk in the episode about what leads people to do bad things with other people's money, even if they're good people, even if they didn't mean to be bad.
turns.zh: 能做到三度做客的人可不多。本期我们探讨了是什么让人们在别人身上的钱上做起坏事来——哪怕他们是好人，哪怕他们并非有意作恶。

turns.en: What leads them to do that? And we talk about why even someone who thinks that they're generally ethical and moral doesn't mean that they're safe from falling down that bad path.
turns.zh: 是什么驱使他们那样做？我们也谈到，为什么即便一个自认为大体上有伦理、有道德的人，也未必能免于滑上那条歧途。

turns.en: We also talked about how investors can try to identify where those risks lie when they're working with professionals. Let's stick around until the end and you'll hear our thoughts in the conversation.
turns.zh: 我们还谈到，当投资者与专业人士打交道时，可以如何试着识别这些风险藏在何处。请留听到最后，你会听到我们对这场对话的看法。

turns.en: So for now, let's get to the episode. Dr. Moira Summers, welcome back to the Rational Minder Podcast and Philippa Hahn, welcome to the Rational Minder Podcast.
turns.zh: 那么现在，进入本期节目。Moira Somers 博士，欢迎回到《Rational Reminder》播客；Philippa Hann，欢迎来到《Rational Reminder》播客。

turns.en: Thank you. So good to be here. We're super excited to be talking to you guys about your new book, The Fault Lines of Finance, Understanding and Preventing Financial Misconduct, which Cameron and I both thought was fantastic from our perspective as practitioners.
turns.zh: 谢谢，能来太好了。我们——Cameron 和我——都特别兴奋能就你们的新书《The Fault Lines of Finance: Understanding and Preventing Financial Misconduct》和你们二位对谈；从我们从业者的角度看，我和 Cameron 都觉得这本书棒极了。

turns.en: We're very excited to be talking to you about the book. Thank you. To kick it off and give listeners some context and background, what is financial misconduct?
turns.zh: 我们很兴奋能就这本书和你们聊聊，谢谢。为了开场并给听众一点背景和铺垫，什么是金融不当行为（financial misconduct）？

turns.en: I would describe financial misconduct. In my opinion, it is doing bad things with other people's money. We have this concept in the book of other people's money because it's really important when you are working in finance that you remember it's not your money.
turns.zh: 我会这样定义：在我看来，金融不当行为就是拿别人的钱做坏事。我们书里有"别人的钱"这个概念，因为在金融行业工作，你必须记住——那不是你的钱，这一点非常重要。

turns.en: So it's doing bad things with other people's money, whether that's trying to take it for yourself or guiding or advising somebody to direct their money in a way which is just not in their best interests.
turns.zh: 所以，就是拿别人的钱做坏事，无论是想把它据为己有，还是引导、建议某个人把钱用到并不符合其最佳利益的方向上。

turns.en: And what motivated each of you to write a book about financial misconduct? I spent 20 years suing financial advisers, wealth managers and banks.
turns.zh: 那么，是什么促使你们各自去写一本关于金融不当行为的书？我花了二十年起诉金融顾问、财富管理人和银行。

turns.en: In doing that, I kept asking myself, when you're looking on the inside of somebody else's inbox, which is what you do during the disclosure process and you're reading all the threads, you're seeing the decisions in real time, if you like, the memos, the transcripts of conversations, the emails that are going on, you've got your client giving you their witness statement when you get to court, you've got the other side giving evidence as well,
turns.zh: 在这个过程中，我一直在问自己——当你在披露程序里翻看别人收件箱的内幕时（那正是你会做的事），读着所有的邮件往来线索，实时看到那些决策：备忘录、对话记录、正在发送的邮件，你从客户那里拿到证人陈述，到法庭上对方也举证，

turns.en: you've seen their witness statement. It was easy in my early years when I was in my late 20s and I'm running these big litigation cases to almost categorize people in a kind of Disney way, if these people are good and these people are bad.
turns.zh: 你看过他们的证人陈述。在我早年、快三十岁、正操盘这些大型诉讼案的时候，我几乎能用一种迪士尼式的方式给人分类：这些人是好人，这些人是坏人。

turns.en: So I always happen to be acting for the good guys and gives the bad guys. It's not that simple. And so as I went through my career, I just kept seeing the same things.
turns.zh: 于是我总是恰好替好人一方，去打坏人一方。事情没那么简单。随着我职业生涯推进，我不断看到同样的现象。

turns.en: I kept having conversations with people on the other side of a courtroom or the other side of a mediation room. And I mean, I met some psychopaths, but largely they were not psychopaths.
turns.zh: 我不断和法庭另一侧、或者调解室另一侧的人对话。我是遇到过几个精神病态者，但绝大多数并不是。

turns.en: And I just had this niggling question of why did it happen? There was an easier option. There was something that was clear that they should have done and they didn't take it.
turns.zh: 我总有一个挥之不去的疑问：为什么会发生这种事？明明有一条更容易的路，明明有件显而易见他们该做的事，他们却没去做。

turns.en: I wanted to understand why, but when you're a lawyer, no one's paying you to ask questions like that. So I had to wait until I stopped being a lawyer.
turns.zh: 我想搞明白原因，但当你做律师时，没人付钱让你问这类问题。所以我只能等到我不再当律师之后。

turns.en: When I stopped being a lawyer, I just had this desire to answer that question, why do good people do bad things with other people's money? And I had also been at the top of my firm.
turns.zh: 当我离开律师行业，我就特别想回答那个问题：为什么好人会拿别人的钱做坏事？而且我也曾身处律所的顶层。

turns.en: I was an equity partner. I was on the board. I was on the executive committee or was running a large division of 120 lawyers. I had several tens of million pounds that I was responsible for.
turns.zh: 我是权益合伙人（equity partner），在董事会，在执行委员会，负责一个有一百二十名律师的大部门。我要对好几千万英镑负责。

turns.en: And I felt the pressures. I felt the value of being someone that brings in an amazing new client, the adoration of someone that puts in a big bill.
turns.zh: 我感受过那种压力，感受过作为一个带来绝佳新客户的人的价值，感受过开出一张大账单时被人仰慕的感觉。

turns.en: I also felt like the shame and the fear and the upset of being not the top of the pile. And so really the desire to write the book was try to understand why it happens and try to save myself from being one of those people.
turns.zh: 我也感受过那种羞愧、恐惧和难受——不在塔尖的感觉。所以写这本书真正的动力，是想搞明白这一切为什么发生，也想救我自己，别让我成为那种人。

turns.en: I saw Moira at a conference. And I don't know if anybody else saw the light bulb go off above my head when I saw her speak. And I said to myself, that's the lady I need to come and help you write this.
turns.zh: 我在一场会议上看到了 Moira。我不知道别人有没有看到我脑袋上亮起的那只灯泡——我听了她演讲后，心里就说：这位女士正是我需要请来帮我写这本书的人。

turns.en: Wow, Moira? For both of us, there was both a prevention and a promotion aspect or aspirations for the book. Certainly I wanted to do something that could prevent the harms that I was seeing instead of just being called in to patch things up.
turns.zh: 哇，Moira？对我们俩来说，这本书既有"预防"也有"促进"这两层意图或期许。我当然想做一些能预防我所看到的那些伤害的事，而不是仅仅在事后被叫来收拾残局。

turns.en: Because I'm often called in sometimes by regulators, sometimes by insurers, sometimes just by families to deal with the fallout of the fraud or the financial abuse or whatever it's been.
turns.zh: 因为我常常被请去——有时是监管方，有时是保险公司，有时就是那些家庭——来处理欺诈、金融虐待或诸如此类事件造成的善后。

turns.en: So what could we do that could prevent some of this from happening? But I think both of us also wanted to help promote positive changes within the sector as a whole, moving beyond the low hanging fruit of do no harm into a more inspiring notion of helping people do amazing things in their careers in financial services.
turns.zh: 所以，我们能做些什么来预防其中一些事情的发生呢？但我想我们俩也都想帮助整个行业推动积极的变化，超越"无害化"这种低垂的果实，走向一种更鼓舞人心的理念：帮助人们在金融服务的生涯里做出非凡之事。

turns.en: I happen to have the inside scoop on your firm. I know that you folks are among the people who care so profoundly about your clients and who want to help create great outcomes in their lives.
turns.zh: 我恰好对你们的事务所内部情况有所耳闻。我知道你们是这样一批人：如此深切地关心你们的客户，想在客户的生活里促成美好的结果。

turns.en: And when you see people who have that kind of motivation, you just wanna see it contaminate the whole sector, the whole industry in a positive way.
turns.zh: 当你看到有这样动机的人，你就希望它去感染整个行业、整个产业——以正面的方式。

turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting. You both bring such unique perspectives to the topic. I had not really considered, Moira, that you would be working with families in those situations who had been defrauded or who had been the victim of financial misconduct because we've always worked with you in the capacity of people who have lots of wealth and are trying to figure out how to use it to improve their life as much as possible.
turns.zh: 是啊，很有意思。你们二位为这个话题带来了如此独特的视角。Moira，我以前真没想过你会和那些被欺诈、或成为金融不当行为受害者的家庭一起工作，因为我们跟你合作一向是面对那种拥有大量财富、想弄清楚如何用它尽可能改善生活的人。

turns.en: But of course, it makes sense that you would have to deal with situations, I guess the opposite end of that spectrum. Sometimes it's not the opposite end.
turns.zh: 但当然，你要处理光谱另一端的情形也说得通——我猜是那端的反面。有时候它并不是那端的反面。

turns.en: People who have lots of money are amazing prey for people who wanna get down. And how many times have we talked about the psychology of money over the years?
turns.zh: 拥有大量财富的人，正是那些想坑人者的绝佳猎物。这些年来我们聊过多少次金钱的心理（psychology of money）啊？

turns.en: That it brings out so much emotion. And so another actual definition, I guess, of financial misconduct is using your own personal power to control people financially.
turns.zh: 它会唤起如此多的情绪。所以，另一个对金融不当行为真正贴切的定义，也许是：用你自身的个人权力在经济上控制别人。

turns.en: Even if it's with sort of their consent, using money as an instrument of control, it might not be professional misconduct, but it is kind of personal misconduct within the family sphere, for example, or the friendships sphere.
turns.zh: 即便是某种程度上他们"自愿"的——把金钱当作控制的工具，这也许不算职业不当行为，却是家庭范畴、或朋友范畴里的某种个人不当行为。

turns.en: So that too becomes something that it's necessary to unpack when we think about what leads people to do unethical things. I do wanna talk about that because the way you guys approach it, I think is just fascinating.
turns.zh: 所以当我们思考是什么驱使人们做出不道德之事时，那也是一个必须拆解的议题。我确实想谈谈这个，因为你们二位的切入方式，我觉得太迷人了。

turns.en: But before we go there, can you talk about why financial services specifically seems to be susceptible to financial misconduct? Let's talk about the situation that largely leads to professional misconduct.
turns.zh: 不过在深入之前，你们能谈谈为什么金融服务这个行业似乎尤其容易滋生金融不当行为吗？我们来谈谈主要导致职业不当行为的那种处境。

turns.en: We went back and had a look at all the reports from the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners. And the number one red flag for the last, I think 14 years, which is the entire collection of the global report of all the fraud investigators who have looked at people doing bad things with money, and that is financial problems.
turns.zh: 我们回头查看了注册舞弊审查师协会（Association of Certified Fraud Examiners）的所有报告。我认为过去十四年——也就是全部舞弊调查人员研究"人们拿钱做坏事"的全球报告整个汇编期间——排名第一的危险信号，就是财务问题。

turns.en: Financial problems are the biggest issue. So let's put that in one box. If you are not in control of your finances, if you're living beyond your means, if you are in debt, then you are one of the most highly likely people to be involved in some sort of financial misconduct.
turns.zh: 财务问题是最大的因素。我们把它放进一个框里。如果你掌控不好自己的财务，如果你入不敷出、负债累累，那么你就属于最可能卷入某种金融不当行为的那类人。

turns.en: Add into that the fact that the financial services industry gives you access to influencing people with their money. So it provides the opportunities that being a doctor doesn't, for example, or even being a lawyer doesn't.
turns.zh: 再叠加一个事实：金融行业让你在人们的钱上拥有影响力——它提供了一些机会，而做医生、甚至做律师都不会有这些机会。

turns.en: You don't really touch other people's money. You add those two things in together. Then the third one is you are working with money. You are in a world where people don't go to financial plans when they don't have money.
turns.zh: 你并不真正接触别人的钱。把这两件事加在一起。第三，你是在与钱打交道的世界里工作。在这个世界里，人们没钱时不会去做理财规划。

turns.en: They go when they have money. It's a potential way to earn a lot of money and potentially attracts people that think that earning a lot of money is important and then being thrown into a world where lots of people have lots of wealth and then that feels very normal and it feels like something you should have and it feels like something you want.
turns.zh: 他们是有钱时才去。这是一个可能赚大钱的途径，因而可能吸引那些认为赚大钱很重要的人；然后把你扔进一个人人都有大量财富的世界，那感觉很正常，感觉那是你该拥有的、是你想要的。

turns.en: You also throw into that the fact that we're not as rational as we think we are. So it's a whole big recipe of things that means that the financial services industry, unfortunately, is an area where that financial misconduct is more likely to happen because you have all of those elements of it.
turns.zh: 你再叠加上一个事实：我们并不像自己以为的那样理性。所以，是一整大堆因素的配方，使得金融服务这个行业不幸成为金融不当行为更易发生的地方，因为你把上述所有要素都凑齐了。

turns.en: Sounds like trust and opportunity really kind of boils down to people tend to trust people who are in a financial services type role and then there's an opportunity because you're close to the money.
turns.zh: 听起来信任和机会，其实归结为：人们倾向于信任处于金融服务角色的人，然后又存在机会，因为你离钱很近。

turns.en: But also, there's that information inequality as well. It's a bit like that white coat. You know, I don't go into a garage and argue with the mechanic.
turns.zh: 但其中还有那种信息不对称。有点像那件白大褂（white coat）。你知道的，我不会走进一家修车厂去跟技工争辩。

turns.en: I say, well, if you say I need a widget, I believe you because I don't know enough about it and I believe that you are there to help me. So it's a very similar thing.
turns.zh: 我会说：你说我需要某个零件，那我就信你，因为我对它了解不够，而且我相信你是来帮我的。这是非常相似的情形。

turns.en: The more emotion that people have around a topic and heaven knows that money evokes emotion, the more likely it is that you will get extreme responses of either huge difficulty trusting, in which case you probably will never see those people or it will take a very, very long courtship to get involved with them.
turns.zh: 人们对一个话题的情绪越强烈——老天知道金钱能唤起情绪——你就越可能得到极端的反应：要么是极难信任对方，那样你大概永远见不到这些客户，或者要经历非常非常漫长的"追求期"才肯与你合作。

turns.en: Or they come in and they just sort of say, here, kind of like you do to a doctor, I've got all this. I don't know what to do with it. Can you just tell me what to do with it?
turns.zh: 要么他们走进来，差不多就像你对医生那样，把一切交给你：我有一大堆这个，我不知道该怎么处理，你就直接告诉我该拿它怎么办吧。

turns.en: There's lots of evidence that the critical aspects of their brain actually go offline. They look very much when you put them in neuroimaging like the brains of people in prayer.
turns.zh: 有大量证据表明，他们大脑里批判性思考的那些关键部分实际上会"离线"。当你把他们放进神经影像（neuroimaging）里，他们看起来很像祈祷中的人的大脑。

turns.en: The brains of people under conditions of getting financial advice look a lot like the brains of people at prayer. They feel safe, they feel trusted, they feel open.
turns.zh: 接受财务建议时人们的大脑，很像祈祷时的人的大脑。他们感到安全，感到被信任，感到敞开。

turns.en: Like I've got my hands out, like I'm just ready to receive what it is you have to tell me. And so that non-critical aspect, especially for people who aren't particularly financially sophisticated, can ripen the vulnerability.
turns.zh: 就像我摊开双手，随时准备领受你要告诉我的东西。于是那种非批判的状态，尤其对金融上不甚精通的人而言，会酝酿出脆弱性。

turns.en: I think I remember that from your last book, Mara. Fascinating that people's brains just shut off when they're in that conversation with an expert.
turns.zh: 我想我从你上一本书里记得这一点，Moira。人在与专家进行那样的对话时大脑就"关机"了，太有意思了。

turns.en: I definitely experienced that with my clients. And honestly, if I had a pound for every time one of my clients said to me, I didn't ask the question.
turns.zh: 我在我的客户身上绝对经历过这种。老实说，如果我的客户每对我说一次"我没问那个问题"就给我一英镑就好了。

turns.en: I should have understood more and I didn't ask the question. And even, I mean, I used to act for even hedge fund managers who didn't ask the question.
turns.zh: 我本该多了解一些，可我没能问那个问题。甚至——我是说，我曾为一些对冲基金经理打官司，他们也没问那个问题。

turns.en: And they were financially savvy, you would expect them to be. But as Mara said, they sat back and allowed somebody to tell them the answer rather than to have in any form of curiosity about how the product worked.
turns.zh: 他们在财务上很精明，你本以为他们该如此。但正如 Moira 所说，他们往后一靠，让别人替他们给出答案，而不是对产品如何运作抱有任何形式的好奇。

turns.en: Philip, I'd like to go back to your comment about, this isn't necessarily about the Disney style of good versus bad personas. So what does the evidence actually tell us about who commits financial misconduct?
turns.zh: Philippa，我想回到你那句话——这不一定是迪士尼式的好人vs坏人角色那套。那么证据实际上告诉我们，是什么样的人会做出金融不当行为？

turns.en: Yeah, I would love to be able to say it's people with dark hair who wear glasses. It could be any of us is the real answer. But I think it is, we walk around saying, I would never do that or people who do that are just bad.
turns.zh: 是啊，我倒真希望能说，是那些黑头发戴眼镜的人。真正的答案是：可能是我们任何人。但我想，我们四处说"我绝不会做那种事"，或者说"做那种事的人就是坏"。

turns.en: They're just bad and therefore I don't have to think about it anymore or they're just greedy. None of that is true. So I think the truth is it could be any of us.
turns.zh: 他们就是坏，所以我不必再想它，或者他们就是贪婪。这些都不成立。所以我想真相是：可能是我们任何人。

turns.en: And as I said before, as a equity partner in a law firm, I felt that pressure. I felt the need to impress. I felt the desire to hit my targets.
turns.zh: 正如我之前说的，作为律所的权益合伙人，我感受过那种压力，感受过那种必须给人留下印象的需要，感受过那种要达成业绩指标的渴望。

turns.en: I think it is people who don't look after their ethical health who are at risk, if I'm really honest. And it's as broad as that. Moira, what do you think?
turns.zh: 老实说，我认为真正的风险在于那些不照顾自己伦理健康（ethical health）的人，范围就这么宽。Moira，你怎么看？

turns.en: I think that we also need to go beyond the level of the individual Cameron and think about what system are they involved in? One of the early experiences that I had in watching somebody get embroiled in financial misconduct was a young woman.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们还需要超越个体的层面，Cameron，去想想他们身处的是怎样的系统。我早期目睹有人卷入金融不当行为的经历之一，是一个年轻女性。

turns.en: It's a company that's still in existence. I cannot believe it, but it's kind of like a pyramid scheme for financial advising. As a team leader, you go and recruit people who want to help people with their finances.
turns.zh: 那是一家至今仍在运营的公司，我简直不敢相信。它有点像金融顾问领域的金字塔式计划（pyramid scheme）。作为团队领导，你去招募那些想帮人理财的人。

turns.en: So she got brought into this, into this bad system. She was financially unsophisticated herself. And so it was a world that was opening up to her about I could help people.
turns.zh: 于是她被带入这个糟糕的系统。她本人金融上并不成熟。所以对她而言，那是一个正在打开的世界：我可以帮助人们。

turns.en: I could help people in my rural community by selling them these products that are going to just safeguard them. And of course, we all know the products that this company sells are not in the client's best interest.
turns.zh: 我可以帮助我乡村社区里的人，靠给他们卖这些"能守护他们"的产品。当然，我们都知道这家公司卖的产品并不符合客户的最佳利益。

turns.en: I had, at the time, a young man who'd been in a horrible accident at the age of 19, received a multimillion dollar settlement, got approached by one of these people, and got all of his money involved in these funds.
turns.zh: 我当时还有一个年轻男性，十九岁时遭遇了一场可怕的事故，拿到一笔数百万美元的赔偿金，被这些人之一找上，把他所有的钱都投进了这些基金。

turns.en: And it took a lawsuit to get him out of it. So at the same time that she was excited about a career path, I was helping a patient get out of that firm.
turns.zh: 结果要打官司才把他从中拉出来。所以在她为一个职业道路兴奋的同时，我正在帮一位病人摆脱那家公司。

turns.en: And there was not a titch of malice in her. She was all enthusiasm. She had no idea that the company she was keeping was bad, that the system she was in was full of bad incentives and people who did not teach her to ask the right questions and didn't provide a proper education to her.
turns.zh: 她身上没有一丝恶意。她满是热忱。她根本不知道她所效力的那家公司是坏的，不知道她身处的那个系统满是糟糕的激励，也没人教她该问对的问题、没给她应有的教育。

turns.en: And so it's not what we talk about time and time again in the book is that ethics isn't just a solo sport. It is a team sport and heaven help you if you get involved in an organization even in a bank in Canada, the US, that decides to ask you to start doing things that are not in clients best interests because you may not know any different.
turns.zh: 所以，我们在书里反复谈到的就是：伦理不只是一项单人运动，它是一项团队运动。老天保佑，如果你加入一个组织——哪怕是在加拿大、美国的一家银行——它开始要求你做一些不符合客户最佳利益的事，因为你可能根本不知道有区别。

turns.en: And they don't tell you that. They don't tell you this isn't in the client's best interest. They tell you that it is or that it's good for the client.
turns.zh: 他们不会告诉你这一点。他们不会说"这对客户不符合最佳利益"。他们会告诉你它符合，或者说这对客户有好处。

turns.en: Like you said, they'll convince you that you're helping people. My first job in financial services, that was part of the training and the coaching is that we are helping people.
turns.zh: 就像你说的，他们会说服你你是在帮人。我在金融服务行业的头一份工作，训练和辅导里就有这一条：我们是在帮助人们。

turns.en: And to an extent it's probably true, but you're also incentivized to sell really high-fee products that if you knew better, you would understand or probably not in the client's best interest.
turns.zh: 某种程度上大概确实如此，但你同时也被激励去卖那些高费率的产品，如果你更懂行，你就会明白——那大概并不符合客户的最佳利益。

turns.en: It reminds me of how I met my husband. It was in a karate class in the very first class. They put me into boxing gloves and they pointed at this guy and they said, go hit him.
turns.zh: 这让我想起我是怎么认识我丈夫的。是在一堂空手道课上。头一节课，他们给我戴上拳击手套，指着那个男的，说：去，打他。

turns.en: And I said, okay. And I tried to go hit him. They told me to do that. When you go into a new company or a bank and they say, sell somebody this credit card or sign them up for this credit card, you go, okay.
turns.zh: 我说：好啊。然后我就试着去打他，因为他们让我那么做。当你新加入一家公司或一家银行，他们让你去跟某人推销这张信用卡、或让人办这张信用卡，你就说：好啊。

turns.en: Cause that's what you were just told to do. That was your job. And you don't even know how to approach the issue really. If you're just hired cold off the street and all of the training is done in-house and you don't have any particular qualifications, you're not regulated, this is part of why the financial field is right for misconduct as well.
turns.zh: 因为他们刚让你那么做，那就是你的工作。你甚至不知道该怎样去处理这件事。如果你是刚从街上"生招"进来、所有培训都在公司内部完成、你没有任何特定资质、也不受监管——这正是金融领域适合不当行为滋生的部分原因。

turns.en: It's such a patchwork of regulations and lack of regulations. We talked about, I guess, a lack of training or education. We talked about incentives, but you guys go so much deeper in the book.
turns.zh: 它是监管与缺监管的一种大杂烩。我们谈到缺乏培训或教育，谈到激励，但你们在书里挖得深得多。

turns.en: Can you talk about some of the other reasons that good people, like you mentioned in that story, you just told Meira, this is a good person doing bad things.
turns.zh: 你能谈谈还有哪些原因会让好人——就像你在那个故事里讲的，你刚跟 Moira 说的——"这是个好人做了坏事"——还有哪些别的东西会让好人拿别人的钱做坏事？

turns.en: What are some of the other things that can lead good people to do bad things with other people's money? People can stumble into it through simply following orders.
turns.zh: 人们可以仅仅因为服从命令而误入歧途。

turns.en: We have a whole chapter divided to misguided helpfulness. So trying to be helpful and not understanding that you are crossing boundaries that you must not cross because it just feels like you're doing good or because it feels withholding to not do the thing that you're being asked to do.
turns.zh: 我们书里专门有一章讲"被误导的乐于助人"（misguided helpfulness）。就是想要帮忙，却不明白你在越过一些绝不该越过的界线，因为那种帮忙让你感觉自己在做好事，或者不照被要求的那样做会让你觉得像是吝于给予。

turns.en: Both sides of that aspect of helpfulness. Another topic that we take on is not knowing what to do when you've made a mistake. Has anybody in this call not made an ethical mistake at some point?
turns.zh: 关于"乐于助人"这个特质的两面。我们涉及的另一个话题是：当你犯了错，你不知道该怎么办。在这次连线里，有谁从来没有犯过一个伦理错误吗？

turns.en: Probably not. I mean, we've probably all stumbled at some point, but what do you do when that happens? Mostly we're just told don't do it and we're not told what to do when you do do it.
turns.zh: 大概没有。我是说，我们大概都有过失足的时候，但当那种事发生时，你该怎么办？我们大多只被告知"别那么做"，却没被告知当你真的那么做了该怎么办。

turns.en: And so the impulse is to hide and to just make that bad feeling stop. And that desire to make it stop leads people to do things that just get them in deeper and deeper and deeper.
turns.zh: 于是本能反应就是隐藏，就是让那种糟糕的感觉停止。而那种"让它停下来"的欲望，会让人做出把他们越拖越深、越陷越深的事。

turns.en: We have the story of John in the book who was exactly that, wasn't he? And it was such an innocent mistake. He was new in the job and he received an email from a client saying, call me, it's urgent.
turns.zh: 我们书里有 John 的故事，说的正是这个，对吧？那是一个多么无辜的错误。他刚入职，收到客户一封邮件说：给我打电话，急事。

turns.en: It was one of those clients, we've all had one of those clients, and they're demanding and they are aggressive and they just want the right answer right now.
turns.zh: 就是那种客户——我们都遇到过那种客户——他们咄咄逼人、态度强硬，只想立刻得到正确答案。

turns.en: And in his heart of hearts, he was just a bit afraid that he did some other stuff that he could do and he knew he could do a good job in it and went home at the end of the day, hadn't called him.
turns.zh: 而他内心深处，只是有点怕，他其实可以去处理别的工作、他知道那件事他能做好，于是下班回了家，没给他回电话。

turns.en: Next day, same thing. Did the stuff he knew he could do. Happy feeling comfortable doing that stuff. And then eventually when the client contacted his boss and said, why haven't I received a call and his boss speaks to him?
turns.zh: 第二天，同样如此。他做了那些他知道能做好的事，做着那些让他感到舒服、开心的事。直到最后，那位客户联系了他的老板说：我怎么一直没接到电话？老板来问他。

turns.en: In the moment, he lies. I didn't get an email and then goes back and doubles down on it. And I told that story at a conference about six months ago and a few weeks later, I was at another conference and one of the advisors who'd been there said to me, you wouldn't believe this, Philippa, but exactly the same thing happened in my firm.
turns.zh: 在那一刻，他撒谎了——"我没收到邮件"，然后又回去加倍地圆这个谎。大约半年前，我在一个会议上讲了这个故事，几周后我在另一个会议上，一位当时在场听过的顾问对我说：真不敢相信，Philippa，我们事务所里发生了一模一样的事。

turns.en: This was a really great firm with a really good culture. He said, exactly that's why I've sat down and said to him, you need to watch Philippa's talk because this stuff happens and it's that kind of in the moment thing where you are panicking and your brain literally isn't working properly.
turns.zh: 那是一家非常好的、文化很好的事务所。他说：正因如此我坐下来对他说，你得去看看 Philippa 的演讲，因为这种事真的会发生，就是那种当下你慌了神、你的大脑根本不正常工作的情形。

turns.en: How do you think financial professionals should calibrate their moral compasses? My view is that a lot of these problems, as Moira has just said, come from that decision-making in the moment.
turns.zh: 你们觉得金融从业者该如何校准他们的道德指南针？我的看法是，很多问题——正如 Moira 刚说的——都来自那种当下瞬间的决策。

turns.en: So when you're going into work, you're not necessarily looking out for that ethical dilemma. You're not on high alert. Actually, you're just trying to get through the day, get through your emails, prepare your annual planning meetings, do all the stuff that you're doing, meet the client, do your jobs.
turns.zh: 所以当你去上班时，你未必在提防那个伦理困境。你并非高度戒备。其实你只是想过完这一天，处理你的邮件，准备你的年度规划会，做你手头的各种事，见客户，干你的活。

turns.en: You're not looking out for this stuff. It can catch you off guard. So in the book, we create a design your own moral operating system effectively, which we worked super hard on to make sure that people could actually take it away and work through step by step who they are, what their vulnerabilities are.
turns.zh: 你没在留意这些东西。它能让你措手不及。所以在书里，我们让人设计一套属于自己的"道德操作系统"（moral operating system），我们下足了功夫，确保人们真能把它拿走，一步一步地梳理自己是谁、自己的脆弱点在哪里。

turns.en: That's the kind of thing that we're looking at because you might be someone who is a huge people pleaser. You know, lots of people are, and in the moment you find yourself vulnerable because you don't want to say no to someone or you don't want to say, that looks a bit dodgy.
turns.zh: 这正是我们在审视的那种情形，因为你也许是个巨大的讨好者（people pleaser）。很多人都是。在当下，你会发现自己很脆弱，因为你不想对某人说"不"，或者你不想说"那看起来有点可疑"。

turns.en: I mean, how often do you want to have those conversations? Not often. And if you know that you are someone who is a people pleaser or maybe you are just exhausted, you're just exhausted and you just want it to stop.
turns.zh: 我是说，你们多久会想说那些话一次？不常。如果你知道你是个讨好型人格，或者你只是精疲力竭——你就是累了，只想让这一切停下来。

turns.en: You just want to get through your emails. You just want the person to stop being crossed with you, whatever it is. Or maybe you are reliant on the firm to pay your mortgage or your rent.
turns.zh: 你只想把邮件处理完，只想让那个人别再对你发火，无论是什么。或者也许你依赖这家公司来付你的房贷或房租。

turns.en: And actually you being able to house your family is dependent on you saying yes to whatever it is you're being asked to do. So one of the things that we suggest in the book is that you understand what your own personal vulnerabilities are.
turns.zh: 而你能够养家，取决于你对被要求做的任何事说"好"。所以我们在书里建议的其中一点，是去理解你自己的个人脆弱点是什么。

turns.en: And then actually you plan around that stuff. So if you are dependent on the next paycheck to pay your rent or your mortgage, you better get working to make sure that you have some money in the background that means that you can say no.
turns.zh: 然后你真的围绕这些去做规划。所以如果你要靠下一张工资支票来付房租或房贷，你就最好开始着手，确保你在背后有些钱，让你能说得出"不"。

turns.en: Or if you are a people pleaser, I am a massive people pleaser. I hate saying no to people. So I have to have in my back pocket just some wording that says, oh, hang on a minute.
turns.zh: 或者如果你是个讨好型人格——我就是个超级讨好者，我讨厌对人说不——所以我兜里得备着几句话："哦，等一下，我得回去想想，我明天再回复你，好吗？"

turns.en: I just need to go away and think about that. Can I come back to you tomorrow, for example? It's having things in your toolkit that means that you are ready for it when it happens.
turns.zh: 就是让你工具箱里有些东西，好当事件发生时你已经有所准备。

turns.en: Another important part of that is journaling. When have I felt uncomfortable? When have I been put in a position where I've walked away from a conversation and thought I didn't say what I was thinking or I've agreed to something that feels uncomfortable?
turns.zh: 其中另一个重要部分是写日记（journaling）。我什么时候感到不舒服？我什么时候被置于一种境地，离开一场对话时心想"我没说出我心里想的"，或者"我答应了某件让我觉得别扭的事"？

turns.en: That kind of thing. Journaling is an incredibly powerful thing. So we run through a 12 step actually moral operating system for people to do on their own.
turns.zh: 就是这类事。写日记是一件极其强大的事。所以我们梳理了一套十二步、真正的道德操作系统，供人们独自去做。

turns.en: Or we recommend actually with others, you can sit down and test and ask questions and work through it together. We've both done it and it's a really interesting thing to do.
turns.zh: 或者我们更推荐与人一起——你可以坐下来，测试、提问、一起把它走完。我们俩都做过，这是一件非常有趣的事。

turns.en: And when you have to name your own non-negotiables. So my non-negotiables, for example, are I don't lie, I don't pretend I know something when I don't and I apologize when I need to.
turns.zh: 而当你要说出你自己的"不可妥协原则"（non-negotiables）。比如我的不可妥协原则是：我不撒谎；我不在不懂时装懂；该道歉时我会道歉。

turns.en: That last one's really hard. But I find myself bumping up against them more than you would imagine. But because I know what they are, at that point I can stop myself and think, why am I tempted to tell a lie at that point?
turns.zh: 最后一条真的很难。但我发现自己撞在这些原则上，比你想象的更频繁。正因为我知道它们是什么，在那个节点我能叫停自己，想一想：我此刻为什么想撒谎？

turns.en: What's going on for me? And I am still training. This is a journey of a lifetime. Those things are really important in us looking after our ethical health.
turns.zh: 我身上在发生什么？我仍在训练之中。这是一生的旅程。这些东西对我们照顾自己的伦理健康真的很重要。

turns.en: Mario, do you have any thoughts on that one? Knowing your own vulnerabilities is a particularly challenging one. But I tell you what, the psychopaths out there, they will find your vulnerabilities so fast, they're so good at it.
turns.zh: Moira，关于那一点你有什么想法吗？了解自己的脆弱点，是特别有挑战的一件事。但我告诉你，外面那些精神病态者，他们会以惊人的速度找到你的脆弱点，他们太擅长这个了。

turns.en: If you look at con artists, do you know what the con and con artists stands for? Confidence. They know how to get you to be confident in them.
turns.zh: 如果你看看骗子，你知道"con artist"（骗子）里的 con 代表什么吗？Confidence，信心。他们懂得如何让你对他们产生信任。

turns.en: That's why people end up doing outrageously trustful things with people is because they know how to make you feel confident in them. Mapping out, where is it in the past that you might have been tricked by somebody?
turns.zh: 正因如此，人们最后会对着别人做出令人咋舌的轻信之举，因为他们懂得如何让你觉得可以信赖他们。去梳理一下：过去在哪里，你也许曾被人骗过？

turns.en: Or where is it that you would just really like yourself to go offline and just be taken care of? What are the points of seduction? Maybe you have a lot of ambition.
turns.zh: 或者在哪里，你就是真想让自己"关机"、被人照顾？那些"诱惑点"是什么？也许你野心勃勃。

turns.en: Maybe you like the shiny things. There's no judgment in this. It's just self-knowledge. And the more self-knowledge you have, the better equipped you are to protect yourself from people who don't have your best interests at heart, or indeed to protect yourself from your own impulses.
turns.zh: 也许你喜欢那些光鲜的东西。这里面没有评判，只是自知之明。你越有自知之明，就越有准备去保护自己，免受那些并不为你着想之人的伤害，或者说，免受你自己冲动的伤害。

turns.en: Eugene Soltis is an author that I quite enjoy following. He wrote a book called Why They Do It, and it's essentially an expose on white-collar crimes.
turns.zh: Eugene Soltis 是一位我挺喜欢关注的作者。他写过一本叫《Why They Do It》的书，本质上是对白领犯罪的揭露。

turns.en: What he found was that these aren't people who sit down with a prose and a cons list, and they painstakingly work out. It's really worth it for me to engage in that.
turns.zh: 他发现，这些人并不是坐下来列一列利弊清单、一丝不苟地盘算：我做那件事真的值。

turns.en: Most of these people, it was an impulse. It was a momentary decision to just do the thing, to hide, to lie on the income statement that they had to give to the chair of the board.
turns.zh: 他们大多数，那是一时冲动，是当下就去做那件事、去隐藏、在对董事会主席提交的损益表上撒个谎的决定。

turns.en: It wasn't well thought out. It was poor impulse control because they were tired, they were pressured. Everybody wanted a piece of them, and they maybe didn't know what to do.
turns.zh: 它不是深思熟虑的，那是糟糕的冲动控制，因为他们累了、他们压力大、人人都要分他们一杯羹，他们也许不知道该怎么做。

turns.en: And so that mapping out of what would I do in these circumstances? How do I prevent myself from getting in these circumstances? And who are my people?
turns.zh: 所以要梳理：在这些情形下我会怎么做？我该如何防止自己陷入这些情形？我的人是哪些人？

turns.en: Who are the people that I can pick up the phone and call when I am struggling with an issue? And I don't know what the right thing to do is, or even worse, when I do know what the right thing to do is, but I don't wanna do it, because it's gonna be hard.
turns.zh: 哪些人是当我被一个问题困扰、不知道正确的做法是什么时，可以拿起电话打给他们的？甚至更糟的是，当我确实知道正确的做法是什么、却不想去做，因为它会很难时。

turns.en: So identifying who are your people that will solidly stand behind you as you do the right thing. You tell the story of Tom Hardin in the book, who we had on this podcast in episode 398.
turns.zh: 所以要找出，当你做正确之事时，哪些人会坚定地站在你身后。你们在书里讲了 Tom Hardin 的故事，他上过我们这档播客第398期。

turns.en: You talk with us in the book too about how he did call people, but he kinda used it as- He used it for confirmation bias, is what he used it for.
turns.zh: 在书里你们也谈到，他的确打电话找人商量了，但他其实是把它用作——他把它用成了确认偏误（confirmation bias），那是他的用法。

turns.en: Yeah. When psychology, one of our ethical guidelines is, if you're concerned about somebody else's conduct, the conduct of a colleague, you have to reach out to that colleague directly.
turns.zh: 是啊。在心理学里，我们有一条伦理准则：如果你担心别人——同事的行为举止，你必须直接去联系那位同事。

turns.en: Oh, that's hard. That's really hard. The notion is that you've gotta strengthen yourself to have hard conversations. I uncovered misconduct in one of the family offices that I'm working with.
turns.zh: 哦，那太难了。真的很难。其理念在于，你得让自己变强，好去进行艰难的对话。我在跟我合作的一家家族办公室里发现过不当行为。

turns.en: This just happened a couple of months ago. It was obvious that somebody that everybody loved was going to have to be let go. And I had to call up Philippa and say, oh my God, I hate this.
turns.zh: 这事就发生在几个月前。很明显，一个人人喜爱的人将会不得不被解雇。我不得不打给 Philippa 说：天哪，我讨厌这样。

turns.en: I hate this. This wasn't a psychopathic person. This wasn't a narcissistic person. This was somebody who was trying to do the right thing and went horribly wrong.
turns.zh: 我讨厌这样。这不是一个精神病态者，不是自恋者。这是个本想做正确之事、却彻底走偏了的人。

turns.en: I had to call up Jim Grubman and Philippa and say, help me see what I'm not seeing or help me conceptualize this in a way so that when the rubber hits the road, I can do the right thing.
turns.zh: 我不得不打给 Jim Grubman 和 Philippa 说：帮帮我，看看我漏掉了什么，或者帮我把这件事重新框定一下，好当事到临头时，我能做正确的事。

turns.en: And they were very helpful. And what a privilege to be that person for someone else. It is so much easier to see it for someone else than it is to see it for yourself.
turns.zh: 他们非常乐于助人。能为另一个人成为那样的一个人，是一种多大的荣幸。为别人看清，比为自己看清要容易太多了。

turns.en: We sort of ended up sort of a bit aghast because this is the stuff we've been writing about. And it was happening to Moira. And so that was wild actually to see the book in action.
turns.zh: 我们俩最后有点目瞪口呆，因为这正是我们一直在写的内容，而它却发生在了 Moira 身上。所以看到这本书"落到实处"，真的很奇特。

turns.en: That is very cool. We had Jim on, Jim Grubman on an episode 282, I think. You mentioned ambition Moira. And that's one of the things we talked to Tom Hardin about is that his own desire to be successful was one of his big weak points to let him to do what he did.
turns.zh: 那太酷了。我们请过 Jim，Jim Grubman，应该是第282期。Moira 你提到了野心。那也是我们就 Tom Hardin 谈到的事情之一：他自己想要成功的欲望，是他能做出他所做之事的重大弱点之一。

turns.en: Any one of the strengths that we have can be turned into a weakness. Are you confident? Whoop, watch out. Are you ambitious? Whoop, are you not confident?
turns.zh: 我们拥有的任何一种优势，都可能变成一种劣势。你自信吗？哎呀，小心。你雄心勃勃吗？哎呀，你不够自信吗？

turns.en: Whoop, are you very humble? Oh, just knowing yourself and knowing what to do, knowing how that could show up. If you think of how would a spy approach you?
turns.zh: 哎呀，你非常谦逊吗？哦，就是认识你自己，知道该怎么做，知道那会如何显现。你想想，一个间谍会如何接近你？

turns.en: What would Madahari do to seduce you? What would an objective outsider say that your vulnerabilities are? How do you deal with those? And being isolated is one of those vulnerabilities.
turns.zh: 一个马基雅维利（Machiavelli）式的人会如何诱惑你？一个客观的局外人会说你的脆弱点是什么？你如何应对这些？而"孤立"就是脆弱点之一。

turns.en: Having that sounding board outside of yourself. And one of the real difficult places to be is either a new person in a firm which leaves you very isolated and wanting to please or managers, particularly new managers when they're suddenly moving.
turns.zh: 在你之外有那样一个"回音板"（sounding board）。而真正难处的境地之一，是你要么是公司里的新人——那让你非常孤立、很想取悦人；要么你是管理者，尤其是刚升上去、处境突然变动的管理者。

turns.en: I mean, I remember moving into that management position. And feeling like I had to have all the answers, feeling like I had to make all the decisions, feeling like I couldn't make a mistake, et cetera, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我是说，我记得我升到那个管理职位时，觉得自己必须有全部答案，觉得自己必须做全部决策，觉得自己不能犯错，如此如此。

turns.en: And those are, particularly when you're feeling that way, an incredibly vulnerable position. Is that resonating with you, Cameron? Yeah, it sure is.
turns.zh: 而当你正是那种感受时，那是极其脆弱的境地。这跟你有共鸣吗，Cameron？是啊，确实如此。

turns.en: It's so interesting. It's very much the system, right? And the roles inside the system can cause this issue to be exasperated. How you run your firm, how you create an environment for integrity, for relationships is so important when you're running a financial firm.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这很大程度上是系统的问题，对吧？系统中的角色会让这个问题被放大。你如何经营你的事务所，你如何营造一种诚信、一种人际的环境，在你经营一家金融公司时至关重要。

turns.en: One of the cases that we highlight, we sort of divide the book into three sections. So there's sort of what's been wrong with traditional ethics training and what needs to happen to make it better.
turns.zh: 我们书里突出的一个案例——我们把书分成三个部分。第一部分讲传统伦理训练出了什么问题、要怎么做才能更好。

turns.en: What do the regulators want us to know? What does the research evidence say? That's the first part of the book. And then the second part of the book is case studies.
turns.zh: 监管方希望我们知道什么？研究证据怎么说？这是书的第一部分。然后第二部分是个案研究。

turns.en: Study after study of some of the headlines they hit the news, some of the cases that Philippa was involved in, some of the cases that I was involved with as a psychologist.
turns.zh: 一项又一项研究，关于一些上过头条的、关于 Philippa 参与的一些案子、关于我作为心理学家参与的一些案子。

turns.en: Just looking at what was there in the firm that allowed things to go on, in some cases that encouraged bad stuff to go on, or that didn't prevent it.
turns.zh: 就是去看在事务所里有什么，让那些事得以持续，有些情形下甚至鼓励坏事持续，或者没能阻止它。

turns.en: Like having somebody that you trust implicitly as your accountant and you don't require a second signature. Well, that's just setting somebody up if things start going awry in their life, you've just set them up to engage in workplace embezzlement that can go undetected.
turns.zh: 比如你把某个人当作你的会计师、完全信任他，却不要求第二个人签字。那简直就是在设局——如果那人生活中开始出岔子，你就等于设下了让他可以不被发现地实施职场挪用（embezzlement）的局。

turns.en: Yes, it is his fault or her fault, but it's kind of also your fault if you're the business owner and haven't set up better practices. We have to think about the fact that we're working with vulnerable human beings with all of these strengths and weaknesses and that systems have a huge role to play and culture has a huge role to play in whether stuff is ethical or not.
turns.zh: 是的，那是他或她的错，但如果你是那个企业主却没建立更好的做法，那也多少是你的错。我们必须想到，我们打交道的是脆弱的人，带着所有这些长处和短处，而系统扮演着巨大的角色，文化也扮演着巨大的角色，决定事情是否合乎伦理。

turns.en: Even how easy do you make it to surface a mistake? I was just gonna jump on that word culture because, Ben, as you know in our environment, mistakes happen in trading, right?
turns.zh: 甚至，你让"暴露一个错误"这件事变得有多容易？我正要接"文化"这个词——Ben，你知道在我们的环境里，交易中会出错，对吧？

turns.en: And the team knows it's never a bad time to make the right decision. And often you could say, oh, the client would never notice, but everyone here knows, nope, take the high road, always do what's right.
turns.zh: 团队知道，做正确决定的时机永远不嫌晚。很多时候你本可以说"哦，客户永远不会注意"，但这里每个人都知道：不，走正道，永远做正确的事。

turns.en: You know what's right, do what's right. And it's just part of our culture, I believe, right, Ben? Yes, and part of our system is like, we're not punishing people for bringing forward a mistake like that, which I think is how you could get to a place where they would wanna hide it.
turns.zh: 你知道什么是对的，就去做对的。这是我们文化的一部分，对吧，Ben？是的，我们系统的一部分是，我们不会因人们这样上报一个错误而惩罚他们，因为我觉得那正是会让他们想要掩盖错误的做法。

turns.en: Yes, the system will pay for the mistake, not the person. But there's punishment and punishment. So there's punishment of telling someone off or saying you will pay for it and all the rest of it, but there's also punishment in a sigh.
turns.zh: 是的，系统会为错误买单，而不是那个人。但"惩罚"也分两种。有那种斥责某人、说"你来赔"之类的惩罚，但也有藏在一声叹息里的惩罚。

turns.en: There's punishment in a look. All of that stuff, we are sucking in this information all the time, but one of the red flags that you should be looking out for is if people are not making mistakes.
turns.zh: 藏在一个眼神里的惩罚。所有这些，我们无时无刻不在吸收这些信息。但你应该警惕的一个危险信号就是：如果人们从不犯错。

turns.en: Anyone who doesn't make mistakes, I only ask a question to them, what's going on here? Because it's not normal to not make mistakes. Yeah, that's interesting.
turns.zh: 任何人如果从不犯错，我只会问他们一句：这里到底怎么了？因为不犯错才是不正常的。是啊，很有意思。

turns.en: Mara, something that you mentioned a couple of times now that jumped out to me, the way that I read through the book was it's often just regular nice people who are doing bad stuff, but you mentioned psychopaths a couple of times.
turns.zh: Moira，你提到过好几次的一点引起了我的注意——我读这本书的感受是，往往就是普通的好人做了坏事，但你提到过几次精神病态者。

turns.en: How worried should people in everyday life for doing consuming financial services be about psychopaths? The evidence is that they disproportionately gravitate towards financial services and business.
turns.zh: 在日常生活中，接受金融服务的人，应该有多担心精神病态者？证据是，他们不成比例地被金融服务业和商业吸引。

turns.en: It's where the money is. Because that's where the money is. It's like the old story of the bad bank robber getting caught and he was asked, why do you keep robbing banks?
turns.zh: 因为钱在那里。因为钱在那里。就像那个老故事：坏银行劫匪被抓，人家问他：你为什么一直抢银行？

turns.en: And his answer was, well, that's where the money is. So that's where the money is now. And we know that financial services are one of the top two targets for workplace fraud and financial misconduct because that's where the money is.
turns.zh: 他的回答是：因为钱在那里。所以现在钱也在那里。我们知道金融服务业是职场欺诈和金融不当行为的前两大目标之一，因为钱在那里。

turns.en: And so pure psychopaths often aren't very successful, but sort of psychopath light, the snakes in suits. There's a book that's been written by a Canadian, one of the world experts on psychopathy is actually here in Canada, Robert Hare.
turns.zh: 纯粹的精神病态者往往不太成功，但那种"轻度精神病态"、穿西装的毒蛇（snakes in suits），写过这方面的书——是一位加拿大人写的，世界顶尖的精神病态研究专家之一恰恰就在加拿大，叫 Robert Hare。

turns.en: And he talks about what does it look like when you're successful at this? And you tend to be charming. You know how to find people's longings and tap into them.
turns.zh: 他谈到，当你在这方面"成功"时是什么样？你往往很有魅力。你懂得如何发现人们的渴望并加以利用。

turns.en: You know how to court friendship with the right people. You rope them in, you seduce them or you belittle them if you need to. It is a big issue and they are the ones that tend to leave this trail of destruction then.
turns.zh: 你懂得如何与"对的人"建立友谊。你把他们拉进来，你需要时就诱惑他们、或贬低他们。这是一个大问题，而他们往往是那种留下满路破坏痕迹的人。

turns.en: If they've really got really big brains, they often try to mastermind equally big schemes to get people out of the money, but boy, relationally and from a mental health perspective, they wreak havoc.
turns.zh: 如果他们真的脑子很好使，他们往往试图策划同样庞大的骗局来把人的钱弄走，但天哪，从关系上、从心理健康的角度，他们会造成巨大的破坏。

turns.en: And we were discussing this the other day, Moira and I, because people are generally so relieved when the psychopath is no longer in the firm because they are so destructive.
turns.zh: 前几天 Moira 和我还在讨论这个，因为当精神病态者离开事务所时，人们通常大大地松了一口气，因为他们太具破坏性了。

turns.en: They tend to bat and dam hatches, breathe a sigh of relief, provide a reference to say, well, they worked between this date and that date and they turned up.
turns.zh: 他们往往会既往不咎、松一口气，还出一份推荐，说"哦，他在这段日期到那段日期之间工作过，他按时来上班"。

turns.en: Actually, we're all a bit afraid to say, and I think they're a bit of a psychopath and I definitely wouldn't employ them because we're afraid of being sued.
turns.zh: 其实，我们都多少有点不敢说"我觉得他有点像个精神病态者，我肯定不会雇佣他"，因为我们怕被告。

turns.en: And it is a particular problem because you will see that they will move from firm to firm until they find the opportunity or they'll get away with staff and they'll get away with staff and they'll take their yes people with them and they will sink to wherever they can actually get away with whatever it is that they want to do that provides them with that, they get out of it what they want to get out of it.
turns.zh: 而这是一个特别的问题，因为你会看到他们从一家公司跳到另一家，直到找到一个可以蒙混过关的机会，或者他们能从员工手下溜走、从员工手下溜走，他们会把那些应声虫（yes-people）一起带走，他们会沉到任何他们能真正为所欲为、能从中得到他们想要的东西的地方。

turns.en: And it is a real problem because non-psychopaths are just so relieved to have them out of their lives that they walk away and it's understandable.
turns.zh: 而这是一个真正的问题，因为非精神病态者能摆脱他们的生活就太如释重负了，于是他们转身走开，这是可以理解的。

turns.en: Yeah, I think you referenced the paper, I think it's called the market from up financial misconduct as I was called. The market, right? Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想你引用过那篇论文，我记得标题大概是关于不当行为的市场——那个"市场"，对吧？对，就是那篇。

turns.en: The advisors gravitate to certain firms after having conducted misconduct and then they end up. They are recruited, it's not just they gravitate towards it, they are recruited preferentially by certain firms who like to engage in exploitation of vulnerable people.
turns.zh: 顾问们在做出不当行为之后会涌向某些事务所，然后最终——他们是被招去的，不只是他们自己涌去，而是被某些事务所优先招募，那些事务所乐于剥削脆弱的人。

turns.en: How do we become ethical people? Such a nice question after all this. Such an easy question, obvious one. I have a theory around you look after your physical health, you look after your mental health.
turns.zh: 我们如何成为有道德的人？在一堆这样的内容之后，真是个好问题。这么容易、这么显然的一个问题。我有个理论：你照顾身体健康，你照顾心理健康。

turns.en: And I think there is an argument to say, and that's what we conclude in the book, you need to be taking steps to look after your ethical health.
turns.zh: 而我想可以说——这也是我们在书里的结论——你需要主动采取措施来照顾你的伦理健康。

turns.en: Spending some time working on yourself is vital for you to be able to look after your ethical health. And there is this kind of triumvirate, if you like, of weirdly self-esteem.
turns.zh: 花些时间在自己身上下功夫，对你能够照顾好自己的伦理健康至关重要。有一种三者并列的结构，你可以这么说——奇怪的是，自尊（self-esteem）。

turns.en: Because if you have self-esteem, you can say, I don't want to do that, thanks very much, I'm good. People who lack self-esteem tend to go along to get along.
turns.zh: 因为如果你有自尊，你就能说"我不想那么做，多谢，我很好"。缺乏自尊的人往往随波逐流以图相安无事。

turns.en: So developing self-esteem, and in order to develop self-esteem, so there was a research project that they did with some school kids, they realized that kids who have high self-esteem have great exam results or have better exam results.
turns.zh: 所以培养自尊——而为了培养自尊，有一个他们和一些小学生做的研究项目，他们发现自尊高的孩子考试成绩很棒、或考得更好。

turns.en: So they went into schools and they bolstered up these kids and they gave them all this really huge self-esteem and they went and did their exams and they did no better than anyone else.
turns.zh: 于是他们进了学校，给这些孩子"打气"，给了他们非常非常高的自尊，然后他们去考试，结果并不比其他人更好。

turns.en: What they realized as a result was that you don't get good exam results because you have good self-esteem. You have good self-esteem because you've put the work in to have the exam results.
turns.zh: 由此他们意识到的是：你并不是因为自尊高才考得好；你之所以有自尊，是因为你下了功夫才取得那些成绩。

turns.en: So in order to get good self-esteem, you have to put the work in. You need to go and do the exams. You need to go and make sure that your private life is in good shape, that you are tackling the difficult things, that you're having the conversations, that you're attempting those things.
turns.zh: 所以，为了获得好的自尊，你必须下苦功。你得去参加考试，你得确保你的私生活状态良好，你去处理那些难做的事，你去进行那些对话，你去尝试那些事。

turns.en: So self-esteem is really important. Self-compassion is really important, weirdly, that came out of our research. If you are able to say, well, it's okay that I made a mistake because I'm a human being and humans make mistakes and it's okay to go and tell my boss, sorry, I think I made a mistake.
turns.zh: 所以自尊真的很重要。自我关怀（self-compassion）也很重要，奇怪的是，这一点从我们的研究里冒了出来。如果你能对自己说我犯了个错也没关系，因为我是人，人都会犯错，我去告诉我老板"抱歉，我觉得我搞砸了"也没关系。

turns.en: Can you help me? And having enough compassion for yourself to say, can you help me? I mean, if someone goes to you as their boss and says, can you help me please?
turns.zh: "你能帮帮我吗？"——并且对自己有足够的慈悲去说出"你能帮帮我吗"。我是说，如果有人作为你的下属走到你面前说"你能帮帮我吗，求你了"？

turns.en: It's a totally different conversation. In what circumstances are you ever going to say, no, I'm not going to help you? And that self-actualization piece.
turns.zh: 那完全是另一种对话。在什么情形下你会说出"不，我不打算帮你"？还有那个自我实现（self-actualization）的部分。

turns.en: So doing the work on yourself in terms of what are your values? What are your vulnerabilities? How are you going to deal with those? What are your non-negotiables?
turns.zh: 所以在你身上下功夫：你的价值观是什么？你的脆弱点是什么？你打算如何应对它们？你的不可妥协原则是什么？

turns.en: Do you understand yourself? Are you doing the journaling? Do you have your ethical sounding board around you? Do you know where to go and who to speak to?
turns.zh: 你了解自己吗？你在写日记吗？你身边有你的伦理"回音板"吗？你知道该去哪里、该找谁谈吗？

turns.en: There is work which is involved in this, but that work, I promise you, would you know this, is so worth it. Nobody goes into a profession in order to wreak havoc.
turns.zh: 这件事里有辛苦的工作，但那份工作——我向你保证——太值了。没有人进入一个行业是为了制造破坏。

turns.en: People go into a profession to help people and to achieve that sense of self. And in order to avoid the pitfalls, you need to do that work on yourself.
turns.zh: 人们进入一个行业是为了帮助他人、是为了获得那种自我感。而为了避开那些陷阱，你需要做那番对自己的功课。

turns.en: I love that answer. And I think even the willingness to do those things is perhaps seated in us way, way earlier. And I ask you, Cameron, how did you become ethical?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个答案。而且我想，甚至愿不愿意做那些事，也许早就非常非常深地植根于我们之中。Cameron，我想问你：你是如何变得有道德的？

turns.en: When we ask that of the regulators, and I remember coming back and asking you this question, most people, first of all, point to people in very early childhoods.
turns.zh: 当我们问监管方这个问题——我记得回来过、问过你们这个问题——大多数人首先指向非常早期的童年。

turns.en: They talk about their parents, people who taught them from a very young age. They talk about coaches being part of a religious tradition. There's a foundational element to that that says there is right and there is wrong.
turns.zh: 他们谈到自己的父母，那些从很小的时候就教导他们的人。他们谈到教练，谈到身为某个宗教传统的一部分。那里有一个基础性的要素，说的是：有对，也有错。

turns.en: This is what to do. And also, this is what will happen if you don't do the right thing. That's part of the answer to how do we become ethical is that we are taught by people who have our best interest in heart.
turns.zh: 这就是该做的。还有，如果你不做正确的事，就会发生这些。这就是"我们如何变得有道德"的答案之一：我们是被那些为我们着想的人教出来的。

turns.en: And we are also modeled. There's a common saying that values are caught rather than taught. And so we see people around us doing the things or not doing the things that they're counseling us to do.
turns.zh: 我们也是被示范出来的。有句常话说，价值观是被"感染"到的，而不是被"教"会的。于是我们看到身边的人做或不做那些他们劝告我们去做的事。

turns.en: And we see how that work out. Can somebody like me do this kind of thing too for good or for ill? I think then as we get older, we do start to get explicit teaching, especially if we are in a profession that has ethics requirements as part of ongoing certification or whatever.
turns.zh: 我们看到那会产生怎样的结果。像我这样的人也能做成这样的事吗？为了善，还是为了恶？我想随着年龄增长，我们确实开始接受显性的教导，尤其是如果我们在一个把伦理要求作为持续认证或其他环节一部分的行业里。

turns.en: We start learning ethical reasoning. We might be actually taught this is what you do here versus there. This is how to even think ethically.
turns.zh: 我们开始学习伦理推理（ethical reasoning）。我们也许真的被教：在这儿该这样，在那儿该那样。这就是甚至该如何进行伦理地思考。

turns.en: These are some of the thinking skills that are required. Where we found that the ethics breaks down is that it doesn't sufficiently engage the heart.
turns.zh: 这些是所需的一些思维技能。我们发现伦理"断裂"的地方在于，它不足以触动人心。

turns.en: I hate to sort of do that dichotomy, but in other words, it doesn't teach us what to do when it's tough to do the right thing. It just says do the right thing.
turns.zh: 我不想搞那种二元对立，但换句话说，它并没有教我们在做正确之事很难时该怎么做。它只是说"做正确的事"。

turns.en: Oh, well, thanks. That was helpful. Don't cross boundaries. Oh, great. But what if I have or what if it feels like it is ethical to cross that boundary?
turns.zh: 哦，那谢谢了，真有用。"别越界。"哦，太好了。可如果我已经越了呢，或者如果越过那条界看起来反而是符合伦理的呢？

turns.en: What if it feels cold and callous and absolutely heartless to tell a client that I can't do this thing? Well, oh, oh, I'm either hooped or I'm helped because I've had training on what to do.
turns.zh: 如果告诉客户"我没法做这件事"让我感觉冷酷、麻木、铁石心肠，那怎么办？那我是被捆住了手脚、还是被帮到了——因为我受过该怎么做这方面的训练。

turns.en: And I know who I can talk to when it's really, really hard. It's not a solo sport, not from the earliest days that we're on the earth. We're always getting inputs on what it means to be ethical, to be a good person.
turns.zh: 而且我知道在真的、真的很难的时候我可以找谁谈。这不是一项单人运动——从我们来到地球的最初那些日子起就不是。我们始终在接受各种输入，关于做有道德的人、做好人意味着什么。

turns.en: I really love that part of our book, actually. Ethics isn't just about identifying when there's a problem and knowing what to do. It's about having the moral character to actually do something.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢我们书里的这一部分。伦理不只是发现问题所在、知道该怎么做，而是有那种道德品格，真的去做点什么。

turns.en: I think when we were looking at that, it just kind of hit me like a freight train, that it's so true, not just knowing what the right answer is, but having the character, the motivation, ability, desire to feel uncomfortable to do the right thing at the same time was such a big thing when we were writing that.
turns.zh: 我想当我们审视那一点时，它像一列货运火车一样撞醒了我：这是真的——不只是知道正确答案，还有品格、动机、能力、愿意在感到不适的同时去做正确之事，这在我们写作时是一件如此之大的事。

turns.en: One of the things that comes up in your case studies, Tom Hardin is a good example where when we had him on this podcast, he tells us whole backstory and you can tell, he's like, he's a good person, he's raised well.
turns.zh: 你们的个案研究里浮现的一件事，Tom Hardin 是个好例子：当他上我们这档播客时，他把整个背景故事讲给我们听，你能感觉到——他是个好人，家教很好。

turns.en: If you asked younger Tom, if you would do the things that he did, he would say, absolutely not, but then he did them. What causes that ethical drift in people over time?
turns.zh: 如果你问年轻的 Tom 会不会做他所做的那些事，他会说绝不会，可后来他还是做了。是什么造成人们随着时间推移的"伦理漂移"（ethical drift）？

turns.en: Or what can cause it? If you talk to him, you will know some of the story, but that is kind of universal. He was in an extraordinarily high pressure environment that did not tell people what right looks like here and what wrong looks like here and what to do if you are tempted to cross the line.
turns.zh: 或者可能造成它的是什么？如果你和他谈过，你会知道一部分故事，但那有点普遍性。他身处一个压力极高的环境，那里没告诉人们在这儿"对"长什么样、"错"长什么样，也没告诉你当你被引诱越线时该怎么做。

turns.en: There was no explicit ethical teaching from the firm leaders on down. There weren't conversations. It was sort of an assumption. Well, don't cross the line.
turns.zh: 公司从上到下没有显性的伦理教导。没有那样的对话。那多少是一种想当然：别越线就是了。

turns.en: He was what, 26 when he started? Maybe not for that particular firm, but right out of college, he went into the hedge fund world at the end.
turns.zh: 他开始工作时大概二十六岁吧？也许不是在那家特定的公司，但他一出大学就进了对冲基金的世界。

turns.en: It's kind of known for its ruthlessness. So if you don't have people explicitly saying this is what right looks like and these are where your temptations are gonna lie.
turns.zh: 那个世界出了名的冷酷。所以如果没有人明确告诉你"这才是对的样子"、"你的诱惑会藏在这里"……

turns.en: We had one of the people that we highlight. She was having dinner with the Bushes and the Reagans. These big names in American politics when she wasn't even 30 yet.
turns.zh: 我们写过一个人，是我们书里突出的一位。她还没到三十岁，就正与 Bush 家和 Reagan 家共进晚餐——那些美国政坛的大人物。

turns.en: And it was just because of her job. It was all very heady. And you start to have a sense of, this is what normal looks like. And she said the notion that, huh, they're 60.
turns.zh: 而那纯粹是因为她的工作。一切都让人头晕目眩。你开始有种感觉：这就是"正常"的样子。她说过那种念头——"嗯，他们都六十岁了。"

turns.en: I'm less than half their age. Maybe I shouldn't be having private tickets in the sports boxes. Maybe that isn't normative. But again, there was nobody that she could talk to about feelings that were sort of embarrassed about sometimes like, what do I do with my envy?
turns.zh: "我还不到他们一半的年纪。也许我不该拿着私人包厢的球票。也许那并不正常。"但同样，没有人可以让她倾诉那些有时让她难堪的感受，比如"我该怎么处理我的嫉妒？"

turns.en: What do I do with the fact that I am feeling really judgy about how this billionaire and their kids just think that they're all that in a bag of chips and that they can just treat us like we're nothing.
turns.zh: "我该怎么处理我确实对某个亿万富翁和他的孩子感到很有评判这件事——他们觉得自己有多了不起，他们怎么能把我们当空气一样对待。"

turns.en: What do I do with those feelings? What do I do with the fact that I wanna be part of that family? Where do we go with that? You can learn how to manage difficult emotions but the impulse to just swat them away like they're nuisance mosquitoes and that we shouldn't bother acknowledging is the very thing that leads us to act out of them at a weak point.
turns.zh: "我该怎么处理那些感受？我该怎么处理我想成为那个家庭一员的事实？我们该拿这些怎么办？"你可以学会管理艰难的情绪，但那种把它们像讨厌的蚊子一样挥开、觉得不必费心承认的冲动，恰恰是让我们在最脆弱的时刻被它们支配而做出行动的东西。

turns.en: So that's what Tom Hardin did. He was surrounded by all of this. He wanted to help a friend. It was well motivated in the moment. He wanted to help a friend who was in a great distress.
turns.zh: 所以那就是 Tom Hardin 所经历的。他被这一切包围。他想帮一个朋友。在那一刻，动机是好的——他想帮一位深陷困境的朋友。

turns.en: And then he realized, oh my gosh, my friend is making crap loads of money and I'm being all high and mighty and not acting on knowledge that I had.
turns.zh: 然后他意识到：天哪，我的朋友在赚大钱，而我还摆出一副清高自持的样子，没有运用我所掌握的信息。

turns.en: Well, that sucks. And so slowly this drift began and he did reach out to people but he didn't reach out by saying, I have a dilemma. This is both sides of it.
turns.zh: 那可真难受。于是这种漂移慢慢开始了，他的确找过人，但他找人时并不是说：我有个两难，这是它的两面。

turns.en: He just talked to people who he says, you know, offhand, they were some of the good guys but he didn't give them the whole fact case. They just said, oh yeah, you're fine.
turns.zh: 他只是随口跟人聊，他说那些人里有一些是好人，但他没给他们完整的事实全貌。他们只是说：哦没事的，你没问题。

turns.en: So we talked to people about how should you do a consult? When you reach out for a consult, what should that look like? What questions do you need to ask?
turns.zh: 所以我们跟人谈过：你该如何做一次"咨询"？当你去寻求一次咨询时，它该是什么样？你需要问哪些问题？

turns.en: What do you need to surface? And part of that includes, what would it look like if I were wrong? Right, like really looking for disconfirming evidence.
turns.zh: 你需要把什么浮现出来？那其中一部分包括：如果我错了，那会是什么样？真的去找那些反证（disconfirming evidence）。

turns.en: So important. Why doesn't traditional ethics training work? For all of those reasons, when you think about even maybe the last time you certified, you did an ethics class for your certification, they tend to kind of serve up ethical dilemmas on a platter.
turns.zh: 太重要了。为什么传统的伦理训练不起作用？出于所有这些原因。当你想想，也许你上一次为认证做伦理课的时候，他们往往把伦理困境像摆在盘子里一样端给你。

turns.en: Like you know you're getting an ethical dilemma in classroom, right? Well, in real life, they don't present themselves like that. Like with some like unclean, unclean leprosy sign in front of them, they just sneak in.
turns.zh: 你在课堂上就知道自己收到的是一个伦理困境，对吧？可在现实生活里，它们不会那样呈现自己。不会像带着什么"麻风病人请勿靠近"的牌子一样摆在面前，它们会悄悄溜进来。

turns.en: If you are not actively asking a question, is there an ethical issue here? And which of us routinely think to ask that? Then it won't even be part of the reasoning.
turns.zh: 如果你不主动问一个问题——"这里有没有一个伦理问题？"——而我们当中有谁会例行地想到去问那个？那么它甚至都不会进入你的推理。

turns.en: Daniel Kahneman talks about this and though he calls it the YCAD problem, what you see is all there is. So you don't think to ask things like, this product provider who's hyping this amazing new product, what aren't they telling me?
turns.zh: Daniel Kahneman 谈到过这一点，他称之为 WYSIATI 问题——What You See Is All There Is，"你所看到的就是全部"。所以你不会想到去问，比如这个产品提供商在炒作一个了不起的新产品——他们没告诉我的是什么？

turns.en: Who's benefiting from this complexity? Cause it's making my eyes cross as I try to read the prospectus. Do I truly understand this or am I gonna tuck and draft behind somebody else's assumed competence and superior knowledge?
turns.zh: 谁从这种复杂中获益？因为它读招股说明书读得我眼睛都斗鸡了。我真的懂这个吗？还是我要躲到别人假定的能力和高深知识背后去人云亦云？

turns.en: Those are some of the things that we found were quite critical. Those were the factors that led people to just kind of go offline. So even if they'd been taught ethical reasoning at some point, it doesn't even get triggered much of the time.
turns.zh: 这些是我们发现相当关键的几样东西。那些是把人变得"离线"的因素。所以即便他们曾在某个时刻被教过伦理推理，大部分时候它甚至都不会被触发。

turns.en: You don't even know that you've got an ethical dilemma. You skate across that line because you're too busy. You're incentivized to do so. You're incentivized to look the other way.
turns.zh: 你甚至不知道自己有了一个伦理困境。你从那条线上一掠而过，因为你太忙了，你被激励着这样做，你被激励着视而不见。

turns.en: But you don't know what questions to ask. I know you've done some really good conversations with Jason Pereira over the years. He talks about that all the time.
turns.zh: 但你不知道该问什么问题。我知道你这些年和 Jason Pereira 做过一些很棒的对话。他一直在谈这个。

turns.en: Most advisors do not really know how to analyze the quality of any of their offerings. They were not trained in statistics. They don't know how to read the papers.
turns.zh: 大多数顾问并不真正知道如何分析他们所提供的任何东西的质量。他们没受过统计学的训练，他们不会读那些论文。

turns.en: They go to court and they feel prepared to attest to the fact that, yes, I was competent to do this and yes, I was acting in the client's best interest and it all falls apart like a house of cards under cross-examination.
turns.zh: 他们上法庭，觉得自己准备好去作证："是的，我够格做这件事，是的，我是在为客户的最佳利益行事"——然后一切在交叉质询（cross-examination）下如纸牌屋般崩塌。

turns.en: Jason has great stories of being an expert witness in those cases and providing the evidence that the advisor did not in fact know what they were doing even if they thought that they did.
turns.zh: Jason 有很多很棒的故事，讲他在这类案子里当专家证人，提供证据表明那位顾问其实并不知道自己所做的事——哪怕他自以为知道。

turns.en: So that gets us to, you better figure out who you want to work for. Because there are a lot of places that don't have your back and saying my firm told me to do it is not a defense.
turns.zh: 这就把我们带到：你最好弄清楚你想为谁工作。因为很多地方并不会为你撑腰，而说"是我公司让我这么做的"并不是一种抗辩。

turns.en: Our hearts are particularly heavy for the young people like the one I mentioned at the outset of this call who don't know what they don't know.
turns.zh: 我们的心特别为那些年轻人沉重——就像我在这次连线开头提到的那位——他们不知道自己不知道什么。

turns.en: You know, there's lots of people giving advice out there who don't even have the basic CFP qualifications or whatever that equivalent is in the UK, Philippa.
turns.zh: 你知道，外面有太多给出建议的人，甚至连基本的 CFP（特许金融策划师）资质都没有，或者——Philippa——在英国有对应的什么资质。

turns.en: They might have a particular license to sell a particular thing, but they don't know how to look at the overall picture and they don't know how to analyze what they're being told to do.
turns.zh: 他们也许有一个卖某样特定东西的执照，但他们不懂得如何看全局，也不懂得如何分析他们被要求去做的事。

turns.en: I remember the first time that I understood how the RRSP and TFSA accounts work. Those are the registered accounts, the tax preferred accounts that we have in Canada, at least two of them.
turns.zh: 我记得我第一次搞懂 RRSP 和 TFSA 账户怎么运作的时候——那是加拿大我们有的一些注册账户、税收优惠账户，至少有这两个。

turns.en: And it was well after I had been licensed to sell mutual funds and insurance, which is terrifying. I remember that light bulb going off and being like, huh, it feels a little bit irresponsible that I was able to sell financial products without understanding this.
turns.zh: 而那已经是我拿到卖公募基金和保险的执照之后很久了，这很吓人。我记得那盏灯泡"啪"地亮了，心想：我能在不理解这些的情况下就卖出金融产品，感觉有点不负责任。

turns.en: I've had many similar confessions on the podcast ban over the years. Like it's embarrassing to look back at my early years and how the industry worked back then.
turns.zh: 这么多年来在播客上我听过太多类似的坦白。回头看我的早年、回头看当年这个行业是怎么运作的，真让人尴尬。

turns.en: Totally embarrassing. It's ridiculous. And I wish I could say that's in our rear view mirror, but in our book, I kind of take on Canada's banks and some of the undercover investigations that were done very, very recently.
turns.zh: 完全尴尬，太荒唐了。我真希望能说那都成过去式了，但在我们书里，我多少点名了加拿大的银行，以及一些不久前做的卧底调查。

turns.en: And the follow-up investigations that were done by the Securities Exchange Commissions and what changes as a result of these? Nothing. One third of people who are selling products at banks acknowledge that they don't really know what they're selling or have sold things that are not in the client's best interests.
turns.zh: 以及证券交易委员会（Securities Exchange Commission）做的后续调查，而这些带来的改变是什么？什么都没有。在银行卖产品的人里，有三分之一承认他们并不真正知道自己卖的是什么，或者曾卖出过不符合客户最佳利益的东西。

turns.en: Yikes! On that topic, what role should regulators play in dealing with financial misconduct? A bigger one. I come from the UK perspective. It's funny, you see a cycle of a tightening of regulation in response to a scandal usually, right?
turns.zh: 哎呀！说到这个话题，监管方在应对金融不当行为上该扮演什么角色？一个更大的角色。我从英国的视角来看。有意思的是，你会看到一个循环：通常是丑闻之后监管收紧，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, so there's a big scandal. So we had the pension misselling scandal back in the sort of late 90s. They tightened regulation. Then we had RDR in 2013 and they did upgrade the requirement for qualification.
turns.zh: 是啊，出了个大丑闻。所以我们在九十年代末有养老金误导销售（pension misselling）丑闻，他们收紧了监管。然后 2013 年我们有了 RDR，他们确实提高了资质的要求。

turns.en: So I think joining the financial services profession is not the same as qualifying as a psychiatrist or psychologist or a lawyer or a doctor.
turns.zh: 所以我想，加入金融服务业，和拿到精神科医生、心理学家、律师或医生的执业资格是不一样的。

turns.en: The bar to entry is, I think, probably too low. But also that tightening of regulation, we're now in the part of the cycle where the government once grows and so they're looking to dumb down the regulations that it isn't in the interest of the general investor who actually probably needs something really super dull, doesn't need to be invested in individual shares, they need to be in some sort of diversified
turns.zh: 我认为入门的门槛大概太低了。但还有那个监管收紧的循环——我们现在处于政府开支膨胀的那一段，所以他们正想把监管降级，可这并不符合普通投资者的利益，普通投资者其实大概需要一些非常非常乏味、不必投资个别股票的东西，他们需要的是某种分散化的……

turns.en: global portfolio, et cetera, et cetera. So their role of the regulator, actually, I think, is to fight against that, to lobby for tighter regulation and actually to be braver, to remove people from the profession itself.
turns.zh: ……全球化投资组合，如此如此。所以我认为监管方真正的角色，是对抗那个趋势，去游说收紧监管，并且真正更勇敢一点，把不合格的人从这个行业里清除出去。

turns.en: I think we don't see enough of that. There's also another part of it for me around what the requirements are for insurance. You can't be a qualified advisor without having the qualifying insurance.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们见得还不够多。对我来说还有另一部分，关于保险的要求。没有那项执业保险，你就成不了合格的顾问。

turns.en: Now, the detail of that qualifying insurance engages the insurers in this question of regulation effectively because if you can't get insurance, then you can't be regulated.
turns.zh: 而那个执业保险的细节，实际上把保险公司也卷入了监管这件事里，因为如果你拿不到保险，你就没法被监管。

turns.en: But if we continue to allow insurers to exclude various products or services, then they will continue to do that and nothing will change. But actually they have a really powerful agent for change.
turns.zh: 但如果我们继续允许保险公司排除某些产品或服务，那么它们会一直那样做，什么都不会改变。可它们其实是一个真正强大的变革杠杆。

turns.en: If your regulator refuses to allow your insurer to exclude certain liabilities, then you can bet damn sure that those insurers will be all over you because they don't want you to be sued.
turns.zh: 如果你的监管方拒绝允许你的保险公司排除某些责任，那你大可断定那些保险公司会死死盯着你，因为他们不想让你被告。

turns.en: They don't want you to be fined. There is that side of it as well, which I think is wildly underutilized by regulators globally. Look at the requirements for lawyers in the UK.
turns.zh: 他们不想让你被罚款。还有这一面，我认为在全球范围内都被监管方严重未加利用。看看英国对律师的要求吧。

turns.en: Insurers cannot exclude liability for products or pieces of advice. And therefore, you are at risk of not getting insurance. If you can't get insurance, then you can't trade.
turns.zh: 保险公司不能对某类产品或某条建议排除责任。因此，你就有拿不到保险的风险；如果拿不到保险，你就没法执业。

turns.en: And it is an extremely powerful thing. We are not using it well enough in the financial services industry, I believe. Really interesting point.
turns.zh: 这是一件极其强大的事。我相信我们没能在金融服务业把它用得足够好。真有意思的一点。

turns.en: Philippa, you mentioned financial problems earlier. What are some other warning signs of possible future misconduct offenders? We talked about early years and so the book is written in large parts of the early years.
turns.zh: Philippa，你前面提到过财务问题。还有哪些可能预示未来不当行为者的危险信号？我们谈过早年阶段，所以书里很大一部分写的就是早年阶段。

turns.en: People, as Moira said, they are people who are bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. We talk about Evan in the book, for example, who within a month of qualifying was in the middle of a global fraud.
turns.zh: 人们——正如 Moira 所说——他们眼睛发亮、生机勃勃。我们书里讲到 Evan，比如，他在取得资质后一个月内，就卷入了一场全球性的欺诈。

turns.en: His qualification lasted about nine months and he was, in fact, banned for life by the UK regulator. So early years is a red flag. Being in debt is a red flag.
turns.zh: 他的资质大概只维持了九个月，他实际上被英国监管方终身禁业。所以"早年阶段"是一个危险信号。负债是一个危险信号。

turns.en: All the vulnerabilities that we talked about earlier, being beholden to your boss to pay your mortgage is a problem. Being a people pleaser is something you need to be careful of.
turns.zh: 我们之前谈到的所有脆弱点，被你的老板拿捏着要还房贷是一个问题。是个讨好型人格，是你要小心的一件事。

turns.en: Being somebody who is low in self-esteem and therefore wants to buy in self-esteem by buying a Maserati or insert name of fancy car, not massively into cars myself.
turns.zh: 一个自尊很低、于是想通过买一辆 Maserati、或随便哪个名牌豪车来"买入"自尊的人——我自己不太热衷车。

turns.en: Somebody who feels the need to keep up with the Joneses, actually. Somebody that hasn't done the work on themselves. Somebody who is tired and just wants the noise to stop.
turns.zh: 一个觉得有必要攀比"跟邻居看齐"（keep up with the Joneses）的人。一个没有在自己身上下功夫的人。一个精疲力竭、只想让那些噪音停下来的人。

turns.en: There's a whole gamut of really human biases. And that's another reason why we wanted to write this book, because I think there's a whole plethora of information out there for the financial services industry about how our clients feel, how our clients behave, what biases affect scarcity, bias, all that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 有一整套真正人性的偏见。那也是为什么我们想写这本书的另一个原因，因为我觉得外面有大量针对金融行业的信息，讲我们的客户怎么感受、怎么表现，讲哪些偏见影响稀缺感等等。

turns.en: And there's very little out there which focuses on the biases of the advisor themselves. That is part of the reason why this entire book is about where those vulnerabilities might be and gives people that guide path to try and identify where their own personal vulnerabilities might be.
turns.zh: 而很少有关于顾问自身偏见的东西。这正是整本书聚焦于这些脆弱点可能在何处的部分原因，它给出一条指南路径，让人们试着找出自己的个人脆弱点在哪里。

turns.en: Actually, one of the things we recommend is that you read this book within a book club so that you can have other people to talk to in a really honest way.
turns.zh: 实际上，我们推荐的其中一件事，是你在一个读书小组里读这本书，这样你就有其他人可以用非常坦诚的方式去交流。

turns.en: I hadn't thought about that. Yeah, I did experience that. And, you know, I love Ben's sort of comment there about how it wasn't until I was so many years qualified, I realized I didn't understand the thing that I was selling.
turns.zh: 我以前没这样想过。是啊，我确实有过那种体验。你知道，我很喜欢 Ben 刚才那番话——他说直到执业多年之后，才意识到自己并不理解他正在卖的东西。

turns.en: And there's a whole plethora, but we hugely recommend that people read this book with other people so that they can do that work together. But the other end of the spectrum from that bright-eyed bushy tail we highlight a category I've dubbed the collapse incompetent.
turns.zh: 那有一整套——但我们强烈建议大家和其他人一起读这本书，好让他们一起去做那番功课。而在那个"眼睛发亮、生机勃勃"的另一端，我们突出了一类我称之为"崩塌型不称职"（collapse incompetent）的人。

turns.en: So this was somebody who might have been very, very good but is being brought down by something. And it could be dementia. We've got lots of people working longer in this profession.
turns.zh: 这是一个也许曾经非常出色、但正被某样东西拖垮的人。它可能是痴呆症。我们这个职业里有越来越多的人工作到更长的年纪。

turns.en: And if they're ahead of the firm, who's going to tell them? It's like the ESOP's fable, who shall bell the cat? I'm not going in there, are you going in there?
turns.zh: 如果他们走在公司前面，谁会去告诉他们？就像那则"谁去给猫系铃铛"（who shall bell the cat）的寓言。我不进去，你要进去吗？

turns.en: That's a real risk factor that an impaired brain is not an insightful brain. You are not going to recognize when this stuff is happening to you.
turns.zh: 那是一个真实的风险因素：受损的大脑不是一个有洞察力的头脑。当这些事发生在你自己身上时，你是认不出来的。

turns.en: You've got to have people around who you can trust to say, I need you to let me know. I remember when my mom said, if you see anything wrong with my driving, you let me know.
turns.zh: 你身边得有些你信任的人，让他们对你说"我需要你告诉我"。我记得我妈说过：如果你发现我开车有什么不对，你要告诉我。

turns.en: And when I'm 80, I'm hanging up my keys and gosh, if she didn't do that proactively. But what do we do for our careers that was that open to feedback?
turns.zh: 而我八十岁的时候，我会主动交出车钥匙——天哪，她当年要没那么主动就好了。可我们为自己的职业生涯做了什么，做到那样能接纳反馈吗？

turns.en: Mostly we're trying to engage in impression management, not tell me the hard stuff. Another one that we took on, this is really a warts and all book, right?
turns.zh: 多数时候我们搞的是印象管理，而不是"告诉我那些难听的真话"。我们处理的另一个——这真的是一本瑕瑜并陈、毫不讳言（warts and all）的书，对吧？

turns.en: Like we dig in and we diagnose in this book and we don't shy away from addictions, family problems. Those are other risk factors that can take people down.
turns.zh: 我们在书里深挖、下诊断，不回避成瘾问题、家庭问题。那些也是能把人拖垮的其他风险因素。

turns.en: You know, when your marriage is falling apart, when your kids are acting in ways that are just horrifying to you, terrifying to you, embarrassing to you.
turns.zh: 你知道，当你的婚姻正在破裂，当你的孩子做出那些让你恐惧、让你害怕、让你难堪的行为时。

turns.en: It's really nice to go to work. It's so nice to go to work. People like you, they thank you. And work can turn into what's called an applauded addiction.
turns.zh: 去上班真好啊，上班太舒服了。像你们这样的人，他们会感谢你。于是工作会变成一种所谓的"被鼓掌喂养的瘾"（applauded addiction）。

turns.en: Yay, good for you. Do more, do more. How about more? And so you end up on this hamster wheel of workaholism because you're really good at it.
turns.zh: 好耶，你真棒，再多做点，再多做点，还要更多吗？于是你走上了"工作狂"的仓鼠轮，因为你真的很擅长这个。

turns.en: And because you like it, often a lot more than you like what's going on at home. Even the certified fraud examiner study that Philippa alluded to earlier, they do highlight family problems as being present in one in 10 of the cases that they work with.
turns.zh: 而且因为你喜欢它，往往比你喜欢家里正在发生的事多得多。就连 Philippa 前面提到的那个注册舞弊审查师研究，也确实在他们处理的案例中把家庭问题列为十分之一里都有出现。

turns.en: And certainly we know that if somebody's stumbling into work every morning smelling like they just fell out of the whiskey barrel, you've got to have some way of saying, let me talk, we need to talk.
turns.zh: 而且我们当然知道，如果有人每天早上摇摇晃晃地来上班，闻起来像刚从威士忌桶里爬出来，你就得有些办法去说：我来跟你谈谈，我们得谈谈。

turns.en: And find out how to get support for people who need it, who are struggling. For the retail investors who are listening, I mean, short of smelling someone's breath to see if they've been drinking or asking if they're having family problems at home, what can retail investors do to identify high risk advisors before these issues materialize?
turns.zh: 并去为需要帮助的、正在挣扎的人找到支持。对于正在听的普通散户投资者——我是说，除了闻闻某人口气看他有没有喝酒，或者问他家里有没有闹家庭问题——散户投资者还能做什么，在这些问题显现之前识别出高风险顾问？

turns.en: I always quote a statistic on this. So I was a lawyer for 20 years, sued a lot of finance people, a lot. So I've never sued a certified financial planner.
turns.zh: 关于这个我总是引用一个统计数字。我做了二十年律师，起诉过很多金融人士，非常多。我从没起诉过一个 CFP（特许金融策划师）。

turns.en: And I have sued a lot of financial people. That doesn't mean they don't get into regulatory problems, but it doesn't tend to be massive. In terms of retail investors being able to identify easily, there isn't a magic silver bullet in any of this stuff.
turns.zh: 可我起诉过很多金融从业者。这不代表他们不会陷入监管麻烦，只是那些通常不是大规模的。至于散户投资者能否轻松识别——这里面没有那颗神奇的银弹。

turns.en: If people have gone to the trouble of certifying themselves, then that is a really good sign. But, you know, I never ran out of work. I had highly intelligent people who were my clients.
turns.zh: 如果人们费心去取得了认证，那确实是一个很好的信号。但你知道，我从来不用担心没活干。我的客户里有非常聪明的人。

turns.en: There really wasn't an easy way to identify the bad guys. Again, that's why we wanted to write this book, because we want everyone to do the work on themselves rather than put the obligation on the retail investor.
turns.zh: 真的没有什么简单办法能识别坏人。这也是我们为什么想写这本书，因为我们希望每个人都去做自己身上的功课，而不是把这份义务压在散户投资者身上。

turns.en: I do think if your advisor is not talking to you about your entire life, then they should be. If they are just talking to you simply about investments and they've never found out about you and your goals and your hopes and your dreams and what you care about and who you are, then that isn't financial planning.
turns.zh: 我确实认为，如果你的顾问没有在跟你谈你的整个人生，那么他本该谈。如果他们只是简单地在跟你谈投资，从没了解过你和你的目标、你的希望、你的梦想、你在乎什么、你是谁——那就不是财务规划。

turns.en: That is just wealth management. And you need to understand the difference between the two. And I'm not saying wealth managers are the bad guys, not at all, but as a retail investor, you do need to understand the difference between what you could get, what you should get, and what you would get if you went to somebody that was looking at you as an entire person, as an entire family, as opposed to a returns first
turns.zh: 那只是财富管理（wealth management）。你需要理解两者的区别。我并不是说财富管理人是坏人，完全不是，但作为散户投资者，你确实需要理解：你能得到的、你应该得到的，以及如果你去找一个把你当作完整的人、完整的家庭来看待的人你会得到的——与那种回报至上的……

turns.en: advice process. A couple of weeks ago, we had Barry Riddle, it's on, as a guest, and he said, I think the status is correct, that he mentioned, Ben, that 90% of financial products are garbage.
turns.zh: ……建议流程，三者之间的区别。几周前我们请了 Barry Riddle 做嘉宾，他说——我想他没记错——Ben，他说百分之九十的金融产品都是垃圾。

turns.en: Oh, he said crap, you can say it, Kevin. I'm just being more polite, taking the high road here. But what can advisors do to avoid becoming enamored with bad financial products?
turns.zh: 哦，他说的是"crap"，你可以这么说，Cameron。我只是更客气、走正道一些。但顾问们能做什么，来避免让自己迷恋上那些糟糕的金融产品？

turns.en: They should be as boring as they possibly can be. It is true, isn't it, to be as boring as you possibly can be, and only once you've exhausted the boring, which actually, I now run a financial planning firm, and we do the most boring investments and advice ever.
turns.zh: 他们应该尽可能做到无聊。真的，尽可能地无聊才对——而且只有在把"无聊"穷尽之后——其实，我现在经营一家财务规划公司，我们做的投资和建议是有史以来最无聊的。

turns.en: Most of our clients just don't need anything exciting. So we talk in the book about this complexity here. It feels really special to be part of, only a few people are being offered this particular exciting opportunity.
turns.zh: 我们大多数客户根本不需要任何刺激的东西。所以我们在书里谈到这种复杂性。成为其中一份子会让你感觉非常特别：只有少数人被提供这个特定的、令人心动的机会。

turns.en: And in the same way as the bank follows the money, it is your obligation to understand exactly how this works. And if it doesn't, if you don't understand it, even if it's the best thing ever, you should not be advising on it.
turns.zh: 而正如银行那句"跟着钱走"，去了解这东西到底怎么运作，是你的义务。如果你做不到、你不懂，哪怕它是史上最好的东西，你也不该对它给出建议。

turns.en: It is literally your job to understand exactly where that money is going, how it is making a return, making sure that that makes sense in your mind as to why that's making a return.
turns.zh: 你的工作就是字面意义上要弄清楚那笔钱到底去了哪里、它是怎么产生回报的，确保在你的头脑里那"为什么会产生回报"说得通。
